Some of the adverse effects of ACE inhibi- tors might be mediated by the immune system, but evidence of specific hypersensitivity reactions seems to be limited. The presence of an IgG antibody to captopril was demonstrated in the serum of 2 of 45 patients taking the drug but the clinical signifi- cance was unclear.1 A reaction resembling serum sickness was reported in a patient given captopril, with deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and symp- toms of rash, arthralgia, epidermolysis, fever, and lymphadenop- athy.2 Eosinophilia has also been reported in a number of pa- tients.3 The formation of antinuclear antibodies and lupus-like reactions have been described.4,5 Treatment with ACE inhibitors (enalapril, captopril, or lisinopril) has been associated with the development of anaphylactoid re- actions in patients undergoing high-flux haemodialysis using polyacrylonitrile membrane (AN69).6,7 The UK CSM has ad- vised that the combined use of ACE inhibitors and such mem- branes should be avoided.8 Similar anaphylactoid reactions have occurred in patients taking ACE inhibitors while being treated for severe hypercholesterolaemia by extracorporeal removal of low-density lipoproteins (LDL-apheresis) with dextran sulfate columns.9 These reactions are thought to be bradykinin-mediat- ed. Prolonging the interval between the last dose of ACE inhibi- tor and dextran sulfate apheresis has averted the reaction;10 suc- cessful prevention has also been reported with the bradykinin receptor antagonist icatibant acetate (p.2324).11 Hypotensive re- actions associated with blood transfusion through bedside leu- coreduction filters in patients taking ACE inhibitors have also been attributed to bradykinin.12 There have also been rare reports of severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, occurring
